thread.title: AU Optronics: A Stock That Trades Below Book And Yields 8.7% - AU Optronics Corp. (NYSE:AUO) | Seeking Alpha

author: Vanaheimr Capital
title: AU Optronics: A Stock That Trades Below Book And Yields 8.7% - AU Optronics Corp. (NYSE:AUO) | Seeking Alpha
text:
Investment Thesis AU Optronics Corp. ( AUO ) trades at a trough multiple of .38 times sales and pays a hefty dividend yield of 8.91%. We have confidence that the business will be able to earn reasonable economic profits. However, the decline in sales and unsustainable dividend make the stock riskier than last year. We think that AU Optronics' fourth-quarter results and guidance will inform us if the stock deserves a second chance or if AU Optronics is a value trap. Until we get the results next month we are neutral on the stock and will not look to start a position. If we can identify a turnaround or meaningful catalyst, then the value opportunity could be worth the risk.
Background AU Optronics Corp., as the company is known today, was formed in 2001 after a merger with Acer Display Technology Inc. AU Optronics specializes in two businesses, primarily the manufacturing of TFT-LCD displays and the secondary solar power solutions business. The vast majority of AU Optronics' revenue comes from its LCD business which has benefited from growth in market share for TV, computer, mobile, and commercial displays. The TV business is its largest single division and AU Optronics creates displays in many sizes which supports advanced technologies like High Dynamic Range (HDR), curved displays, and quantum dot. This business has not seen substantial growth over the past decade as we have seen companies like Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ) and Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) move to more advanced OLED displays and other solutions. There is still a market for LCD displays around the world; however, it is a business that is likely at maturity. Going forward, AU Optronics will need to increase efficiency and margins in order to stay competitive. We think the best way to analyze AU Optronics is through its financials since cash flow and EBITDA can tell you a tremendous amount of information about a manufacturing business.
EBITDA is Difficult to Predict When looking at a capital-intensive manufacturing business, we like companies that have reasonable leverage ratios and a commitment to reinvest in the business in order to achieve scale and drive efficiency. AU Optronics has invested a tremendous amount in capital expenditures over the past few years, approximately $5 billion since 2014, only to see profitability decline even in the face of a growing economy. This is the type of behavior that can often occur in declining industries where competition is fierce. The question is if investing capital in the business results in a reasonable return on investment. In our view, AU Optronics does not have any other choice but to invest substantially to reduce costs. If AU Optronics did not invest, it would lose any competitive pricing advantage and see profitability decrease substantially. The company has seen tremendous variability in EBITDA over the past decade even with its substantial multi-billion dollar investments. We think this is mostly because of supply and demand pressures which are incredibly hard to predict. Many of AU Optronics' customers serve end clients and include TV and computer manufacturers who have to gauge the underlying supply of their products. The variability in a given company's unit sales makes it even more difficult for AU Optronics to manage capacity and predict orders into the future. In a low margin business, this is what we think mostly leads to the company's very volatile EBITDA which is, in our view, a characteristic that is not likely to change.
Source: YCharts
The Dividend is Not Sustainable AU Optronics has seen sales declines, on a constant currency basis, for every month in 2018 compared to the prior year. Revenue is likely to stabilize in 2019. However, the trend has been negative since 2014 when revenue surpassed 13 billion NT$. AU Optronics is expected to report earnings for the fourth quarter and hopefully, it can provide some guidance on if sales will grow in 2019. So far we have seen free cash flow plummet from a recent high in 2017 without a substantial reduction in the dividend. The cash dividend payout ratio is at 242% on a trailing twelve-month basis, which is one of the explanations for the precipitous decline of cash on the balance sheet in 2018. The dividend in our view will need to be cut if sales do not stabilize very soon. Capital intensive manufacturing businesses cannot afford to have their operating cash flow sucked out of the business by oversized dividends without serious liquidity risks. As we mentioned earlier, the next earnings release will be a make or break moment as to whether we look to invest or avoid what could be a value trap.
Source: YCharts
A Dividend Cut Would Be Bullish Longer Term When a high-yielding stock either cuts or eliminates the dividend there is usually a swift selloff as the yield-hungry investors flee the stock in droves. If the business does have the potential to improve over time then investors may take the opportunity to enter at reduced prices. So we are by no means confident that the stock would hold up in the short term with a dividend cut. However, over the intermediate to long term, if the business was able to reinvest its cash instead of paying out so much to shareholders, then we could see considerable capital appreciation. We are more likely to wait for a cut.
Source: AUO
Conclusion AU Optronics Corp. meets a lot of criteria for value investors with the stock trading at .58 times book value with $13 billion in assets and only $6 billion in debt, while generating billions of dollars in net income over the past few years. Looking back over the past decade, however, shows that AUO had 4 consecutive years of losses from 2009 through 2012. We are concerned that AUO will continue to siphon operating cash from the businesses at an unsustainable pace which will increase financial leverage considerably. We think that AU Optronics' fourth-quarter results and guidance will inform us if the stock deserves another look or if value destruction is certain. Until we get the results next month we are neutral on the stock price.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions.
